title: Sampling & Discretization
description: Put a computer in the loop: the zero-order hold, exact discrete state models, the mapping from the s-plane to the z-plane and the choice of sample rate.

study.title: The sampled-data loop
study.body: A computer closes the loop in steps of $T$ seconds. The **A/D converter** samples the error (or $y$), the processor evaluates a difference equation $D(z)$, and the **D/A converter** with a **zero-order hold** (ZOH) keeps $u$ constant until the next sample. The plant itself stays continuous. The sample rate is $f_s = 1/T$, or $\omega_s = 2\pi/T$ in rad/s.

study.title: Explore: the hold and its delay
study.body: The ZOH turns the samples into a staircase. On average the staircase lags the signal by half a sample, $T/2$: at frequency $\omega$ that is a phase lag of $\omega T/2$, or $180°/N$ with $N$ samples per period. Fewer samples per period mean a coarser staircase and more lag, which eats phase margin.

study.title: Discretizing the state equations
study.body: With $u$ held constant over each interval, the state equations can be solved exactly from one sample to the next. The result is a discrete model with $\Phi = e^{\mathbf{A}T}$ and $\Gamma = \int_0^T e^{\mathbf{A}\eta}\,d\eta\,\mathbf{B}$; $\mathbf{C}$ and $D$ stay the same. It is exact at the sample instants (no approximation), because the ZOH really does keep $u$ constant. The eigenvalues of $\Phi$ are $e^{\lambda_iT}$.

study.title: Two standard results
study.body:
- First order, $\dot x = -ax + bu$: $\Phi = e^{-aT}$, $\Gamma = \frac{b}{a}(1 - e^{-aT})$.
- Double integrator, $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = [0 \;\; 1]^T$: the series for $e^{\mathbf{A}T}$ stops after two terms, so $\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & T \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\Gamma = \begin{bmatrix} T^2/2 \\ T \end{bmatrix}$ (a constant acceleration for $T$ seconds).
**Example:** $a = 2$, $b = 4$, $T = 0.1$ s: $\Phi = e^{-0.2} = 0.819$, $\Gamma = 2(1 - 0.819) = 0.363$.

study.title: ZOH-equivalent transfer function
study.body: The same discretization in transfer-function form: $G(z) = \mathbf{C}(z\mathbf{I} - \Phi)^{-1}\Gamma + D$, or directly from $G(s)$ with the formula below. For $G(s) = \frac{a}{s + a}$ it gives $G(z) = \frac{1 - e^{-aT}}{z - e^{-aT}}$: the pole maps as $z = e^{-aT}$ and the DC gain stays 1. The poles always map by $z = e^{sT}$; the zeros do not follow a simple rule.

study.title: From s to z
study.body:
Sampling maps every pole $s = \sigma + j\omega$ to $z = e^{sT}$: radius $|z| = e^{\sigma T}$, angle $\angle z = \omega T$.
- left half-plane → inside the unit circle; imaginary axis → the unit circle; $s = 0$ → $z = 1$
- vertical lines (constant decay $\sigma$) → circles of radius $e^{\sigma T}$
- horizontal lines (constant $\omega$) → rays at angle $\omega T$; $\omega = \omega_s/2$ → the negative real axis
- $\omega$ and $\omega + \omega_s$ give the same $z$: aliasing

study.title: Explore: s-plane to z-plane
study.body: Move a pole pair $\sigma \pm j\omega$ around the s-plane ($T$ = 0.1 s, so $\omega_s$ = 62.8 rad/s). Faster decay pulls the poles toward the origin; at $\sigma = 0$ they sit on the unit circle; positive $\sigma$ pushes them outside. Raising $\omega$ to $\omega_s/2$ = 31.4 rad/s swings them round to the negative real axis.

study.title: Choosing the sample rate
study.body: Nyquist ($\omega_s > 2\omega_{BW}$) is only the bare minimum for reconstructing a signal. For control, the hold delay $T/2$, the computation time and an anti-alias filter all add phase lag, and a coarse staircase makes the response rough. A practical rule (FPE): sample at roughly **20 to 30 times the closed-loop bandwidth**. Much faster gives little extra and needs more computing power and more numerical precision (all poles crowd near $z = 1$).

steps.title: A computer in the loop
steps.body: In a digital controller the error is sampled every $T$ seconds, the processor computes a new control value, and the D/A converter holds it until the next sample. Between samples the controller is blind: it neither sees $y$ nor changes $u$. Everything in this unit follows from that.

steps.prompt: Put what happens during one sample period in order.
items: The processor computes $u[k]$ from the difference equation
steps.explanation: Sample, compute, output, hold. The computation takes some time too, which adds delay; the hold then keeps the value constant over the whole interval. These delays are why the sample rate matters for stability, not just for accuracy.

steps.title: The zero-order hold
steps.body: The hold turns the sequence $u[k]$ into a staircase. Compared with a smooth signal through the sample points, the staircase lags by half a sample on average. So the ZOH acts approximately like a delay $e^{-sT/2}$, a phase lag that grows with frequency.

steps.prompt: A loop has its crossover at $\omega_c$ = {{wc}} rad/s and is sampled with $T$ = {{T|s}}. How much phase lag does the zero-order hold add at crossover (in degrees)?
steps.explanation: Half a sample of delay: $\Delta\phi = \omega_cT/2$ = {{wc}} × {{T}}/2 = {{wc*T/2}} rad = {{deg(wc*T/2)}}°. That comes straight off the phase margin, so a slow sample rate can destabilize a loop that was fine in continuous time.

steps.prompt: A 1 Hz sine is sampled and held. Choose the number of samples per period $N$ so that the hold lags the signal by {{X}}°.
steps.explanation: The hold delays by $T/2$, a phase lag of $360° \cdot \frac{T/2}{1\,\mathrm{s}} = \frac{180°}{N}$. For {{X}}°: $N$ = 180/{{X}} = {{180/X}} samples per period. The orange dashed curve is the signal delayed by $T/2$; the staircase wraps around it.

steps.title: How fast to sample?
steps.body: Sampling at twice the bandwidth (Nyquist) is far too slow for control: the hold alone would add 90° of lag at that frequency. Rule of thumb: sample **20 to 30 times faster than the closed-loop bandwidth**. Then the hold costs only a few degrees and the digital controller behaves almost like the continuous design.

steps.prompt: A closed-loop design has a bandwidth of {{wb}} rad/s. What is the slowest sample rate $f_s$ (in Hz) that follows the rule $\omega_s \ge 20\,\omega_{BW}$?
steps.explanation: $\omega_s = 20 \times$ {{wb}} = {{20*wb}} rad/s, so $f_s = \omega_s/2\pi$ = {{20*wb/(2*pi)|Hz}}, a sample period of {{2*pi/(20*wb)|s}}. Mixing up rad/s and Hz (a factor $2\pi$) is the classic mistake here.

steps.prompt: Sampling at twice the closed-loop bandwidth (the Nyquist rate) is enough for good digital control.
steps.explanation: The Nyquist rate only guarantees that a band-limited signal can be reconstructed by an ideal filter. In a loop, the hold adds a lag of $\omega T/2$, which at $\omega_s = 2\omega_{BW}$ is $\pi/2$ (90°) at the bandwidth, and the response becomes a coarse staircase. That is why 20–30× is used.

steps.prompt: A continuous design has {{PM}}° phase margin at $\omega_c$ = {{wc}} rad/s. It is implemented with sample period $T$ = {{T|s}}. Estimate the phase margin left after the zero-order hold (in degrees).
steps.explanation: The hold adds a lag of $\omega_cT/2$ = {{wc*T/2}} rad = {{deg(wc*T/2)}}° at crossover (computation delay would add more). New margin ≈ {{PM}}° − {{deg(wc*T/2)}}° = {{PM - deg(wc*T/2)}}°.

steps.title: Exact discretization
steps.body: Between samples $u$ is constant, so the solution of $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{B}u$ over one interval follows from the matrix exponential: the free part $e^{\mathbf{A}T}\mathbf{x}[k]$ plus the response to a constant input. This is exact at the sample instants.

steps.prompt: Discretize $\dot x = -ax + bu$ with $a$ = {{a}}, $b$ = {{b}} for a ZOH with $T$ = {{T|s}}.

ask.explanation: $\Phi = e^{-aT} = e^{-{{a*T}}}$ = {{exp(-a*T)||4}}. This is also the discrete pole: the continuous pole $-a$ mapped by $z = e^{sT}$.
$\Gamma = \int_0^Te^{-a\eta}d\eta\cdot b = \frac{b}{a}(1 - e^{-aT})$ = ({{b}}/{{a}})(1 − {{exp(-a*T)||4}}) = {{b/a*(1 - exp(-a*T))}}. For small $aT$ this is close to $bT$ = {{b*T}} (Euler).

steps.prompt: A {{m}} kg mass driven by a force, $\ddot p = F/m$, with states $[p \;\; \dot p]^T$, is sampled with a ZOH at $T$ = {{T|s}}.

ask.explanation: $\mathbf{B} = [0 \;\; 1/m]^T$ and $e^{\mathbf{A}\eta} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \eta \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, so $\Gamma = \frac{1}{m}\begin{bmatrix} T^2/2 \\ T \end{bmatrix}$. First entry: $T^2/(2m)$ = {{T^2/(2*m)}} (the distance travelled under a unit force held for $T$).
$\Gamma = \frac{1}{m}[T^2/2 \;\; T]^T$; second entry $T/m$ = {{T/m}} (the velocity gained under a unit force held for $T$).

steps.title: Poles map by $z = e^{sT}$
steps.body: The eigenvalues of $\Phi = e^{\mathbf{A}T}$ are $e^{\lambda_iT}$. So a continuous pole $\sigma \pm j\omega$ becomes a discrete pole with radius $e^{\sigma T}$ and angle $\pm\omega T$. Stable poles ($\sigma < 0$) land inside the unit circle.

steps.prompt: A continuous pole at $s = -{{sg}} + j{{w}}$ is sampled with $T$ = {{T|s}}.

ask.explanation: $|z| = e^{\sigma T} = e^{-{{sg}} \times {{T}}}$ = {{exp(-sg*T)}}. Only the real part of $s$ sets the radius.

ask.prompt: Find the angle of $z$ in degrees.
ask.explanation: $\angle z = \omega T$ = {{w}} × {{T}} = {{w*T}} rad = {{deg(w*T)}}°. Only the imaginary part sets the angle; at $\omega = \omega_s/2$ it would reach 180°.

steps.prompt: Match each s-plane feature to its image in the z-plane.
steps.explanation: $z = e^{sT}$: $|z| = e^{\sigma T}$ is below 1 exactly for $\sigma < 0$ and equal to 1 on the imaginary axis; $s = 0$ gives $e^0 = 1$. A fixed $\sigma$ fixes the radius. The angle $\omega T$ reaches $\pi$ at $\omega = \pi/T = \omega_s/2$.

steps.prompt: The z-plane plot shows the closed-loop poles of a digital control system with $T$ = {{T|s}}. Read their position and estimate the 2 % settling time.
steps.explanation: The poles are at about {{r*cos(th)}} ± j{{r*sin(th)}}, so $|z| = \sqrt{ {{r*cos(th)}}^2 + {{r*sin(th)}}^2 }$ ≈ {{r}}. From $|z| = e^{\sigma T}$ ($\sigma$ the real part of the s-plane poles): $\sigma = \ln|z|/T$ = {{ln(r)/T}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $T_s \approx 4/|\sigma|$ = {{-4*T/ln(r)|s}}. Equivalently: the envelope shrinks by $|z|$ per sample and needs about {{-4/ln(r)}} samples to reach 2 %.

lessons.title: From s to z in practice

steps.prompt: Find the ZOH equivalent of $G(s) = \frac{ {{a}} }{s + {{a}}}$ for $T$ = {{T|s}}, written as $G(z) = \frac{\beta}{z - p}$.

ask.explanation: Scalar model $\dot x = -{{a}}x + {{a}}u$: $\Phi = e^{-aT}$ = {{exp(-a*T)||4}}, which is the pole of $G(z) = \frac{\Gamma}{z - \Phi}$.

$\Gamma = \frac{b}{a}(1 - e^{-aT})$ with $b = a$: $\beta = 1 - e^{-aT}$ = {{1 - exp(-a*T)||4}}. Check the DC gain: $G(1) = \frac{\beta}{1 - p} = 1$, the same as $G(0)$, as it must be for a ZOH equivalent.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{l1}} & 0 \\ 0 & {{l2}} \end{bmatrix}$ is discretized with $T$ = {{T|s}}. Find the bottom-right entry of $\Phi$.
steps.explanation: For a diagonal $\mathbf{A}$, $\Phi = e^{\mathbf{A}T} = \mathrm{diag}(e^{\lambda_1T}, e^{\lambda_2T})$. Bottom-right: $e^{ {{l2}} \times {{T}} }$ = {{exp(l2*T)}}.

steps.prompt: A digital design with $T$ = {{T|s}} must settle (2 %) within {{Ts|s}}. All closed-loop poles must then lie inside a circle of radius $r$ in the z-plane. Find $r$.
steps.explanation: $T_s \approx 4/|\sigma|$ needs a decay rate $|\sigma| \ge 4/T_s$ = {{4/Ts}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The vertical line $\mathrm{Re}\,s = -4/T_s$ maps to a circle of radius $e^{-4T/T_s}$ = $e^{-{{4*T/Ts}}}$ = {{exp(-4*T/Ts)}}. Poles inside that circle are fast enough.

steps.prompt: Closed-loop poles have a damped frequency $\omega_d$ = {{wd}} rad/s and the sample period is $T$ = {{T|s}}. How many samples fall in one period of the damped oscillation?
steps.explanation: The pole angle is $\omega_dT$ = {{wd*T}} rad per sample; a full period needs $2\pi$ rad, so $N = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_dT}$ = {{2*pi/(wd*T)}} samples. With fewer than about 10 the response looks coarse; FPE's rule of 20–30× the bandwidth gives many more.

steps.prompt: With $T$ = 0.5 s ($\omega_s = 4\pi \approx 12.57$ rad/s), which s-plane pole maps to the **same** $z$ as $s = -1 + j2$?
steps.explanation: $z = e^{sT}$ is periodic in $\omega$ with period $\omega_s = 2\pi/T$: $e^{(\sigma + j(\omega + \omega_s))T} = e^{(\sigma + j\omega)T}e^{j2\pi}$. So $-1 + j(2 + 12.57)$ gives the same $z$: the two are aliases. Adding $\omega_s/2$ gives the opposite angle, the conjugate gives the conjugate $z$, and a different real part a different radius.

steps.prompt: $\Phi = e^{\mathbf{A}T}$ is invertible for every $\mathbf{A}$ and every $T$.
steps.explanation: $\det e^{\mathbf{A}T} = e^{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A})T} > 0$, and $e^{-\mathbf{A}T}$ is its inverse. So a discretized continuous plant never has an eigenvalue at $z = 0$: every pole $e^{\lambda T}$ is nonzero. Poles at $z = 0$ only appear when delays are modelled as extra states (computation delay, transport delay) or in the digital controller itself (deadbeat designs).

steps.prompt: A motor $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -{{a}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ {{b}} \end{bmatrix}$ (angle, speed) is discretized with a ZOH, $T$ = {{T|s}}.

ask.explanation: The speed decays as $e^{-at}$ and the angle integrates it: $\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \frac{1 - e^{-aT}}{a} \\ 0 & e^{-aT} \end{bmatrix}$. Top-right: (1 − {{exp(-a*T)||4}})/{{a}} = {{(1 - exp(-a*T))/a}}.

$\Gamma = b\int_0^T\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1 - e^{-a\eta}}{a} \\ e^{-a\eta} \end{bmatrix}d\eta$, first entry $\frac{b}{a}\left(T - \frac{1 - e^{-aT}}{a}\right)$ = ({{b}}/{{a}})({{T}} − {{(1 - exp(-a*T))/a||4}}) = {{b/a*(T - (1 - exp(-a*T))/a)}}.

steps.prompt: The ZOH equivalent of the motor $G(s) = \frac{ {{a}} }{s(s + {{a}})}$ with $T$ = {{T|s}} has two poles ($z = 1$ and $z = e^{-aT}$) and one zero. Find the zero.
steps.explanation:
With $E = e^{-aT}$ = {{exp(-a*T)||4}}: $\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \frac{1-E}{a} \\ 0 & E \end{bmatrix}$, $\Gamma = \begin{bmatrix} T - \frac{1-E}{a} \\ 1 - E \end{bmatrix}$ (here $b = a$), $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$.
$G(z) = \mathbf{C}(z\mathbf{I} - \Phi)^{-1}\Gamma = \frac{\gamma_1(z - E) + \phi_{12}\gamma_2}{(z - 1)(z - E)}$, so the zero is at $z = E - \frac{\phi_{12}\gamma_2}{\gamma_1} = -\frac{1 - E - aTE}{aT - 1 + E}$ = {{-(1 - exp(-a*T) - a*T*exp(-a*T))/(a*T - 1 + exp(-a*T))}}.
It lies just inside $-1$ for fast sampling: sampling creates a zero that has no continuous counterpart.

steps.prompt: A loop crosses over at $\omega_c$ = {{wc}} rad/s. The hold may cost at most {{X}}° of phase margin. Find the longest allowed sample period $T$.
steps.explanation: Hold lag $\omega_cT/2 \le$ {{X}}° = {{rad(X)}} rad, so $T \le 2 \times {{rad(X)}}/{{wc}}$ = {{2*rad(X)/wc|s}}, i.e. $f_s = 1/T \ge$ {{wc/(2*rad(X))|Hz}}. Computation delay would tighten this further.

steps.prompt: A design asks for continuous-time poles with $\zeta$ = {{zt}} and $\omega_n$ = {{wn}} rad/s. Where should the discrete closed-loop poles go for $T$ = {{T|s}}?

ask.prompt: Find the angle of $z$ in degrees.

steps.prompt: $\dot x = -ax + bu$ ($a$ = {{a}}, $b$ = {{b}}) is discretized with $T$ = {{T|s}} and starts at $x[0] = 0$; a unit step $u[k] = 1$ is applied. Find $x[{{k}}]$ by iterating $x[k+1] = \Phi x[k] + \Gamma u[k]$.
steps.explanation: $\Phi = e^{-aT}$ = {{exp(-a*T)||4}}, $\Gamma = \frac{b}{a}(1 - \Phi)$ = {{b/a*(1 - exp(-a*T))||4}}. Iterating gives $x[k] = \frac{b}{a}(1 - \Phi^k)$, here {{b/a*(1 - exp(-a*k*T))}}. That equals the continuous step response $\frac{b}{a}(1 - e^{-at})$ at $t = kT$ = {{k*T|s}}: the ZOH model is exact at the samples.

steps.prompt: Sampling a stable continuous system always gives a stable discrete model, whatever $T$ is.
steps.explanation: Every eigenvalue maps as $z = e^{\lambda T}$ with $|z| = e^{\mathrm{Re}(\lambda)T} < 1$ for $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda < 0$ and any $T > 0$. The open-loop plant stays stable. What a slow sample rate can destabilize is the **closed loop**, through the extra phase lag of the hold.
